title: Measurement Basics
description: Errors, accuracy, precision and resolution, error propagation and how meters load the circuits they measure.

study.title: Error, accuracy, precision, resolution
study.body:
The **error** of a measurement is the measured value minus the true value; it is often quoted as a percentage of the full-scale value $x_{full}$.
- **Accuracy**: the largest expected difference between measured and true value.
- **Precision**: how closely repeated readings of a constant measurand agree (small random error).
- **Resolution**: the smallest change the instrument can show (e.g. one display digit).
The readings below are precise but not accurate: tightly grouped, all about 0.5 V too high.

study.title: Systematic and random errors
study.body:
**Systematic (bias) errors** are the same every time you repeat the measurement: offset, scale (gain) error, nonlinearity and hysteresis. They can be found and removed by **calibration** against a better standard, but they drift with temperature and age.
**Random errors** differ from reading to reading and average to zero. They are reduced by **averaging** repeated readings, never by calibration. (Dashed line: ideal instrument.)

study.title: Propagation of errors
study.body:
When a result is computed from several measured quantities, their uncertainties combine.
- **Sum or difference**: the **absolute** uncertainties add.
- **Product or quotient**: the **relative** (%) uncertainties add; a power $x^n$ multiplies the relative uncertainty by $|n|$.
These worst-case rules assume all errors line up. For independent random errors the root-sum-square (e.g. $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\,\%$) is a more realistic estimate.
**Pitfall:** the difference of two nearly equal readings has a large **relative** uncertainty.

study.title: Loading by a voltmeter
study.body:
A real voltmeter is an ideal meter in parallel with its input resistance $R_V$. Connected across $R_2$ of a divider it puts $R_V$ in parallel with $R_2$, so it reads **less** than the true voltage. The error is small only when $R_V \gg$ the Thévenin resistance seen at the measurement points ($R_1 \parallel R_2$ here).
An ammeter adds its internal resistance in series, so it reads too little current unless that resistance is small compared with the circuit resistance.

study.title: Meter specifications
study.body:
Digital meter accuracy is usually given as $\pm$(% of reading + number of digits). One **digit** (count) is one step of the last displayed digit, i.e. the resolution of the range in use.
Example: a meter showing 12.00 V on its 20 V range (resolution 0.01 V) with spec $\pm(0.5\,\% + 2)$: $\Delta = 0.005 \times 12.00 + 2 \times 0.01 = 0.08$ V.
A $3\tfrac12$-digit meter displays up to 1999 counts, so use the lowest range that still fits the reading.

steps.title: What is an error?
steps.body: Every measurement differs a little from the true value. The **error** is $x_m - x_{true}$ (measured minus true). Instrument makers usually quote it as a percentage of the **full-scale** value $x_{full}$, the largest value the system is designed to measure.

steps.prompt: A pressure gauge with full scale {{xf}} bar reads {{xm||4}} bar when the true pressure is {{xt||4}} bar. Find the (signed) error as a percentage of full scale.
steps.explanation: $\%\,\text{error} = \frac{x_m - x_{true}}{x_{full}}\times 100\,\%$ = ({{xm||4}} − {{xt||4}}) / {{xf}} × 100 % = **{{(xm-xt)/xf*100|%}}**. A positive value means the gauge reads high.

steps.title: Accuracy, precision, resolution
steps.body:
Three different ideas:
- **Accuracy**: how close readings are to the true value.
- **Precision**: how well repeated readings of the same quantity agree with each other.
- **Resolution**: the smallest change the instrument can display.
A meter can be precise without being accurate: every reading is the same, but all are wrong by the same amount.

steps.prompt: Eight readings of a constant 10 V source are plotted below. How would you describe this voltmeter?
options: Accurate on average but not precise
steps.explanation: Look at two things: the **spread** of the readings (precision) and how far their **average** is from the true value (accuracy). Here the spread is about ±{{s|V}} and the average is off by about {{b|V}}. Tight spread = precise; average on the true value = accurate.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning
steps.explanation: Accuracy compares with the **true** value, precision compares readings **with each other**, resolution is a property of the **display/converter** step size, and full scale sets the range that percentage-of-full-scale errors refer to.

steps.title: Systematic vs random
steps.body:
**Systematic** (bias) errors repeat identically: an offset, a wrong gain (scale error), a curved characteristic (nonlinearity) or hysteresis. Calibration against a known standard removes them.
**Random** errors change from reading to reading with zero average, e.g. noise or vibration. Averaging many readings reduces them.

steps.prompt: Which graph of measured value $x_m$ against true value $x_{true}$ shows a **pure scale error**? (The grey dashed line is the ideal $x_m = x_{true}$.)
steps.explanation: A scale error makes the reading proportional to the true value but with the wrong slope: $x_m = k\,x_{true}$ with $k \ne 1$, so the error grows with the measurand and is zero at zero. A parallel shifted line is an **offset**, a curve is **nonlinearity**, and two branches depending on direction are **hysteresis**.

steps.prompt: Averaging many repeated readings removes a constant offset error of the instrument.
steps.explanation: Averaging only reduces **random** errors, which have zero mean. A constant offset is a systematic error: every reading, and therefore the average, contains it. It has to be removed by calibration.

steps.prompt: A meter with a 5-digit display is always more accurate than an otherwise similar meter with a 3-digit display.
steps.explanation: More digits means better **resolution**, not necessarily better accuracy. A 5-digit display can show the wrong value very finely if the meter has a calibration (bias) error.

steps.title: Combining uncertainties
steps.body: Worst case: absolute uncertainties add for sums and differences, relative uncertainties add for products and quotients, and a power $x^n$ multiplies the relative uncertainty by $n$.

steps.prompt: Resistors $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} ± {{t1}} % and $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} ± {{t2}} % are connected in series. Find the worst-case absolute uncertainty of the total resistance (± how many ohms?).
steps.explanation: For a sum the **absolute** uncertainties add. $\Delta R_1$ = {{t1}} % × {{R1|Ω}} = {{R1*t1/100|Ω}}, $\Delta R_2$ = {{t2}} % × {{R2|Ω}} = {{R2*t2/100|Ω}}, so $\Delta R$ = **{{R1*t1/100+R2*t2/100|Ω}}** on a total of {{R1+R2|Ω}} ({{(R1*t1+R2*t2)/(R1+R2)||3}} %).

steps.prompt: Power is found as $P = VI$ from a voltage reading with uncertainty ±{{dV}} % and a current reading with uncertainty ±{{dI}} %. Find the worst-case relative uncertainty of $P$.
steps.explanation: For a product the **relative** uncertainties add: $\frac{\Delta P}{P} = \frac{\Delta V}{V} + \frac{\Delta I}{I}$ = {{dV}} % + {{dI}} % = **{{dV+dI|%}}**.

steps.prompt: The power in a resistor is calculated as $P = V^2/R$, with $V$ known to ±{{dV}} % and $R$ to ±{{dR}} %. Find the worst-case relative uncertainty of $P$.
steps.explanation: $V^2$ doubles the relative uncertainty of $V$, and dividing by $R$ adds that of $R$: $\frac{\Delta P}{P} = 2\frac{\Delta V}{V} + \frac{\Delta R}{R}$ = 2 × {{dV}} % + {{dR}} % = **{{2*dV+dR|%}}**. (Forgetting the factor 2 gives {{dV+dR|%}}.)

steps.prompt: A quantity is the product of two measurements with **independent random** uncertainties of {{a}} % and {{b}} %. Estimate the combined relative uncertainty using the root-sum-square rule.
steps.explanation: Independent random errors rarely line up, so combine them as $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ = $\sqrt{{{a}}^2 + {{b}}^2}$ = **{{sqrt(a^2+b^2)|%}}**, less than the worst case {{a+b|%}}.

steps.prompt: A digital multimeter on its 20 V range (resolution 0.01 V) displays {{vr||4}} V. Its accuracy is ±({{p}} % of reading + {{n}} digits). Find the uncertainty of this reading (± how many volts?).
steps.explanation: % of reading: {{p}} % × {{vr||4}} V = {{p/100*vr|V}}. Digits: {{n}} × 0.01 V = {{n*0.01|V}}. Total: $\Delta v$ = **{{p/100*vr+n*0.01|V}}**, so the true value lies between {{vr-p/100*vr-n*0.01||5}} V and {{vr+p/100*vr+n*0.01||5}} V.

steps.prompt: A voltmeter with input resistance $R_V$ measures the voltage across $R_2$.

ask.explanation: The meter puts $R_V$ in parallel with $R_2$: $R_2 \parallel R_V$ = {{par(R2,RV)|Ω}}. Divider: $v = V_s\frac{R_2\parallel R_V}{R_1 + R_2\parallel R_V}$ = **{{abs(V_RV)|V}}**, while the unloaded voltage is {{Vt|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the loading error (reading − true)/true in percent.
ask.explanation: True (unloaded) voltage: $V_s R_2/(R_1+R_2)$ = {{Vt|V}}. With the meter: {{abs(V_RV)|V}} (from $R_2\parallel R_V$ = {{par(R2,RV)|Ω}}). Error = ({{abs(V_RV)|V}} − {{Vt|V}}) / {{Vt|V}} = **{{(abs(V_RV)-Vt)/Vt*100|%}}**. It is negative: a voltmeter always loads the circuit down.

steps.prompt: An ammeter with internal resistance {{RA|Ω}} is inserted in series with a {{R|Ω}} resistor connected to an ideal {{Vs|V}} source. Find the measurement error (reading − true)/true in percent.
steps.explanation: True current: $V_s/R$ = {{Vs/R|A}}. With the meter: $V_s/(R + R_A)$ = {{Vs/(R+RA)|A}}. Error = $\frac{R}{R+R_A} - 1 = -\frac{R_A}{R+R_A}$ = **{{-RA/(R+RA)*100|%}}**. Small only when $R_A \ll R$.

steps.prompt: To keep loading errors small, a voltmeter should have a very **high** internal resistance and an ammeter a very **low** one.
steps.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in **parallel**, so it should draw almost no current: $R_V \to \infty$. An ammeter is connected in **series**, so it should drop almost no voltage: $R_A \to 0$.

steps.prompt: A sensor has Thévenin resistance $R_t$ = {{Rt|Ω}}. What is the minimum input resistance of the amplifier connected to it if the loading error must be at most {{e}} %?
steps.explanation: The amplifier sees $v_{in} = v_{sensor}\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_t}$. Require $\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_t} \ge 1 - \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon$ = {{e/100||3}}. Solving: $R_{in} \ge R_t\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}$ = {{Rt|Ω}} × {{(1-e/100)/(e/100)||4}} = **{{Rt*(1-e/100)/(e/100)|Ω}}**. Rule of thumb: about $R_t/\varepsilon$.

steps.prompt: A flow sensor's open-circuit voltage is proportional to flow, but its internal resistance changes between {{Ra|Ω}} and {{Rb|Ω}} with fluid conditions. It feeds an amplifier with $R_{in}$ = {{Rin|Ω}}. By how many percent does the overall sensitivity drop when the sensor resistance goes from {{Ra|Ω}} to {{Rb|Ω}}?
steps.explanation: Sensitivity is proportional to $\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_{sensor}}$: {{Rin/(Rin+Ra)||5}} at {{Ra|Ω}} and {{Rin/(Rin+Rb)||5}} at {{Rb|Ω}}. Relative drop = $1 - \frac{R_a + R_{in}}{R_b + R_{in}}$ = **{{(1-(Ra+Rin)/(Rb+Rin))*100|%}}**. A larger $R_{in}$ makes the sensitivity independent of the sensor resistance.

steps.prompt: A resistance is found as $R = V/I$ from $V$ = {{v|V}} ± {{dv}} % and $I$ = {{i|A}} ± {{di}} %.

ask.prompt: Find the worst-case absolute uncertainty of $R$ (± how many ohms?).
ask.explanation: For a quotient the relative uncertainties add: {{dv}} % + {{di}} % = {{dv+di|%}}. $R$ = {{v/i|Ω}}, so $\Delta R$ = {{(dv+di)/100||3}} × {{v/i|Ω}} = **{{v/i*(dv+di)/100|Ω}}**.

steps.prompt: A $3\tfrac12$-digit meter with accuracy ±({{p}} % of reading + {{n}} digits) measures a {{vr|V|4}} signal on its {{rng|V}} range (resolution {{res|V}}). Find the relative uncertainty of the reading in percent.
steps.explanation: $\Delta v$ = {{p}} % × {{vr|V|4}} + {{n}} × {{res|V}} = {{p/100*vr+n*res|V}}. Relative: {{p/100*vr+n*res|V}} / {{vr|V|4}} = **{{(p/100*vr+n*res)/vr*100|%}}**. The digit term matters a lot when the reading is small compared with the range, so pick the lowest range that fits.

steps.prompt: Two node voltages are measured as $v_1$ = {{v1|V}} ± {{u|V}} and $v_2$ = {{v2|V}} ± {{u|V}}. Find the worst-case relative uncertainty of $v_1 - v_2$ in percent.
steps.explanation: For a difference the **absolute** uncertainties add: ±{{2*u|V}} on $v_1 - v_2$ = {{d|V}}. Relative: {{2*u|V}} / {{d|V}} = **{{2*u/d*100|%}}**, although each reading alone is good to about {{u/v2*100|%}}. Measure small differences directly (differential measurement) instead.

steps.prompt: To measure $R_x$, the voltmeter (drawn as its input resistance $R_V$) is connected directly across $R_x$ and an ideal ammeter measures the source current. The result is calculated as $R = v/i$ from the two readings.

ask.explanation: The voltmeter reads $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, but the ammeter carries the current of $R_x$ **and** of $R_V$: $i$ = {{I_Vs|A}}. So $v/i = R_x \parallel R_V$ = **{{Vs/I_Vs|Ω}}**.

ask.prompt: Find the error of this result (calculated − true)/true in percent.
ask.explanation: $v/i = R_x\parallel R_V$ = {{par(Rx,RV)|Ω}} instead of {{Rx|Ω}}: error = $-\frac{R_x}{R_x + R_V}$ = **{{(par(Rx,RV)-Rx)/Rx*100|%}}**. This connection suits **small** $R_x$; for large $R_x$ put the ammeter directly in series with $R_x$ instead.

steps.prompt: A scale reads 0.3 kg with nothing on it, and every reading of a test mass is between 2.29 and 2.31 kg when the true mass is 2.00 kg. What is the best way to improve the result?
options: Use a display with more digits
Nothing: the readings are precise, so they are accurate
steps.explanation: The readings agree within ±0.01 kg (precise) but are all about 0.3 kg high: a **systematic offset**, which is exactly the zero reading. Calibration removes it. Averaging only reduces random scatter, and more digits only improve resolution.
